newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: INTERVIEW - BOTSWANA URGED TO TACKLE UNEMPLOYMENT.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BOTSWANA URGED TO TACKLE UNEMPLOYMENT.

text.p: Botswana must confront its unemployment problem, Mercury Asset Management vice-chairman Richard Dawes said in an interview on Wednesday.

"Botswana needs industries that can satisfy the aspirations of a lot of the younger element of the population. They've gone through a good, well-developed education process, now they need jobs," Dawes told Reuters.
"Botswana must deal with the problem... I am surprised it has not used some of its substantial wealth to encourage manufacturing to a greater extent than it has," he said.
Unemployment in Botswana is officially 21 percent, but this ignores workers on family cattle farms and in the informal sector which brings unemployment to an unofficial 40 percent.
Foreign reserves stood at 18,336 million pula or 25.5 months of import cover as at January 1 against a target of six to eight months. Reserves are forecast to double by the year 2000.
The government also had a cash balance of 700 million pula at the Bank of Botswana as of the same date.

Government policy is that reserves should only be used for sustainable development projects. But the central bank said in its recently published annual economic review that there was a lack of such investment opportunities in Botswana.
Dawes expressed concern at Botswana's economic reliance on (mineral) commodities, its limited stock market and the apparent lack of interest of management for shareholders.
"A problem from the investors' point of view is that Botswana and indeed the entire region is very commodity dominated and this makes markets pretty cyclical," he said.
"But of increasing concern is the lack of awareness by company managements of the interests of shareholders. I don't think that managements recognise that the shareholders actually own the company."
Dawes said Botswanan company managements were not fully accountable to all shareholders, mainly because they tended to be controlled by one dominant group, majority shareholder.

He said Botswana was an interesting market, that geograhically it was in "quite a pole position" in Southern Africa to establish regional industry and that unit labour costs were lower than in South Africa.
